title: Understanding 1 Samuel 28
paragraphs:
Understanding 1 Samuel 28
The Night God Went Silent
There are chapters in Scripture that feel like standing in a thunderstorm.
The wind is violent.
The sky is black.
Every decision feels irreversible.
And when the chapter ends, nobody walks away unchanged.
1 Samuel 28 is one of those chapters.
It is one of the most misunderstood, debated, feared, and emotionally devastating narratives in the entire Old Testament.
Many people read it and immediately ask:
Did Saul really talk to Samuel?
Was the medium of Endor actually speaking with the dead?
Why would God allow this?
What does this chapter teach us about spiritual deception?
What happens when someone spends years running from God and finally discovers heaven has gone silent?
But beneath all the controversy lies something far more terrifying.
This is not primarily a story about a witch.
It is a story about a man who spent years slowly hardening his heart until he could no longer hear the voice of God.
And that should make every believer stop and examine their own soul.
Because 1 Samuel 28 is not merely ancient history.
It is a warning.
A mirror.
A funeral procession for a man who once stood in God's favor and slowly walked away from it.
And perhaps most haunting of all—
Saul did not fall in a single day.
He drifted.
The same way people drift now.
The Silence That Terrified a King
The chapter opens with a national crisis.
The Philistines are gathering for war.
Israel's future hangs in the balance.
Saul sees the enemy army and becomes overwhelmed with fear.
Scripture says:
"His heart trembled greatly." (1 Samuel 28:5)
This is not ordinary anxiety.
This is panic.
This is a man realizing that every decision he made has finally arrived at its destination.
Saul desperately seeks guidance.
He inquires of Yahweh.
But something horrifying happens.
God does not answer.
The Hebrew text says:

וְלֹא־עָנָהוּ יְהוָה
(velo anahu Yahweh)
"Yahweh did not answer him."
Not through dreams.
Not through the Urim.
Not through prophets.
Nothing.
Silence.
Absolute silence.
Imagine praying and hearing nothing.
Imagine begging God for direction and receiving no response.
Imagine standing before the greatest crisis of your life and realizing that years of rebellion have brought you to spiritual isolation.
The terrifying reality is not that God suddenly abandoned Saul.
God had been warning Saul for years.
The silence was the consequence of repeatedly rejecting the voice that had already spoken.
How Saul Arrived Here
To understand 1 Samuel 28, we must understand Saul's journey.
Saul did not begin as a villain.
He began as a humble man chosen by God.
The Spirit of God came upon him.
He prophesied.
He led Israel.
He experienced divine favor.
But slowly pride replaced obedience.
God told Saul to completely destroy Amalek.
Saul partially obeyed.
Then he justified himself.
Then he blamed others.
Then he protected his reputation.
Then he resisted correction.
Then he grew jealous of David.
Then he murdered priests.
Then he pursued innocent blood.
Every step hardened his heart.
Sin rarely destroys people immediately.
It slowly trains the soul to stop listening.
That is Saul's tragedy.
He did not lose God's voice overnight.
He spent years ignoring it.
The Woman of Endor
In desperation Saul seeks something God explicitly forbade.
Ironically, Saul himself had previously removed mediums and spiritists from the land.
Now he secretly searches for one.
The hypocrisy is staggering.
He disguises himself and travels by night to Endor.

The woman is described as possessing an אוֹב
(ov).
The term is difficult to translate precisely.
Most English Bibles render it as "medium."
The word appears throughout the Hebrew Scriptures in contexts involving forbidden attempts to contact spirits or the dead.
God's Law was unmistakable:
"Do not turn to mediums or necromancers." (Leviticus 19:31)
"There shall not be found among you anyone who practices divination or who consults the dead." (Deuteronomy 18:10–12)
The issue was not merely superstition.
It was rebellion.
Seeking spiritual knowledge apart from God's revelation.
Replacing trust in God with counterfeit spirituality.
Seeking control instead of submission.
The same temptation still exists today.
Whenever people pursue spiritual experiences detached from God's Word, they walk the same dangerous path.
The technology may change.
The human heart does not.
Did Samuel Really Appear?
This is where centuries of debate begin.
The text itself presents the figure as Samuel.
The woman is shocked.
Terrified.
Caught off guard.
Whatever happened, it appears beyond her expectations.
The Hebrew text repeatedly identifies the figure as:

שְׁמוּאֵל
(Sh'muel)
Samuel.
The narrative nowhere says it was a demon pretending to be Samuel.
Nor does it describe the event as an illusion.
The figure accurately predicts Saul's defeat and death.
Those prophecies are fulfilled precisely in 1 Samuel 31.
Many faithful scholars therefore conclude that God sovereignly allowed Samuel to appear for judgment, not because necromancy works, but because God chose to intervene uniquely.
Others argue that the appearance was demonic deception.
The text itself leaves certain mysteries unresolved.
What can be stated confidently is this:
The chapter does not endorse communication with the dead.
It condemns it.
The entire event is portrayed as part of Saul's final rebellion.
The Bible consistently forbids attempts to contact the dead.
Nothing in this chapter changes that reality.
Samuel's Final Message
The words spoken are devastating.
Samuel asks:
"Why have you disturbed me?"
Then comes the crushing verdict.
Because Saul rejected God's word, God rejected Saul's kingdom.
David would receive the throne.
Israel would lose the battle.
And Saul and his sons would die.
The next day.
Not years later.
Not eventually.
Tomorrow.
The Hebrew wording carries terrifying finality.
Saul spent years refusing God's warnings.
Now there are no warnings left.
Only consequences.
One of the most chilling truths in Scripture appears here:
There comes a point when opportunities for repentance expire.
Not because God delights in judgment.
But because judgment eventually arrives.
The flood came.
The door of Noah's ark closed.
Jerusalem fell.
And Saul's final day arrived.
The Emotional Collapse
After hearing Samuel's words, Saul falls to the ground.
He is physically weak.
Emotionally shattered.
Spiritually ruined.
This scene is heartbreaking because Saul is not an atheist.
He believes in God.
He knows God's power.
He knows God's commands.
He knows God's history.
Yet knowledge alone cannot save a heart unwilling to surrender.
Many people know about God.
Saul knew about God.
The question has never been information.
The question has always been obedience.
The Gospel Hidden in Saul's Tragedy
At first glance, 1 Samuel 28 seems far removed from the Gospel.
But look deeper.
Saul's story reveals humanity's deepest problem.
Sin separates people from God.
Isaiah later writes:
Saul experiences that separation.
His prayers receive no answer.
His kingdom collapses.
His strength disappears.
His future ends in darkness.
But where Saul's story ends in judgment, the Gospel begins in hope.
At Calvary, Jesus entered the silence Saul feared.
On the cross Christ cried:
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
The Greek text records:

Θεέ μου, Θεέ μου, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες
(Thee mou, Thee mou, hinati me enkatelipes)
Jesus bore the separation sinners deserve so repentant sinners could be reconciled to God.
Saul stands as a warning.
Jesus stands as a rescue.
Saul ran from God until silence remained.
Jesus came so no repentant sinner would ever have to face that silence alone.
That is the difference between religion and redemption.
Religion says, "Try harder."
The Gospel says, "Christ has done what you could never do."
Why This Chapter Still Breaks Hearts Today
Many readers secretly recognize themselves in Saul.
Not because they consulted a medium.
But because they know what it feels like to drift.
To compromise.
To delay obedience.
To ignore conviction.
To postpone repentance.
To assume there will always be another opportunity later.
That is why 1 Samuel 28 remains so powerful.
It forces every reader to ask:
Am I moving closer to God's voice?
Or am I becoming comfortable without it?
Every heart is traveling in one of those directions.
No one stands still.
Some people reading this have spent months pretending everything is fine.
Others have spent years carrying hidden compromises.
Some remember seasons when God's presence felt alive and personal, but now everything feels distant.
The message of 1 Samuel 28 is not merely "Do not become Saul."
The deeper message is this:
Do not wait until tomorrow to respond to God today.
Because the greatest tragedy in Saul's life was not the battlefield.
It was all the years before it.
The years when God was speaking and Saul would not listen.
And perhaps that is why this chapter still echoes through the centuries.
Not because of a medium.
Not because of a spirit.
Not because of controversy.
But because every reader eventually faces the same question Saul faced:
What will you do with the voice of God while He is still calling?
The most dangerous silence is not when God stops speaking—it is when a person stops listening.
